Synopsis: Providing for command and control of State active duty personnel during mobilizations of the Maryland National Guard.
Title: Maryland Military Department – Supervision of State Active Duty Personnel
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/27 at 2:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

bill_summary: This bill clarifies and codifies the chain of command for the Maryland Military Department during state active duty mobilizations. It specifies that all members of the department, including the National Guard and Maryland Defense Force, fall under the operational command and control of the Adjutant General or their designee, even if the Adjutant General is serving in a federal status at the time.
stakeholders: Maryland National Guard members, Maryland Defense Force members, and personnel of the Maryland Military Department
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state or local fiscal impact, as it codifies existing practices regarding command and control during state active duty. There are no projected changes to revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the head of the Maryland Military Department, the Adjutant General is the primary official granted operational command and control of personnel during State active duty under this bill, including provisions for command while in a federal status.

The bill directly concerns the command structure and supervision of National Guard members when they are mobilized for State active duty, clarifying the chain of command between State and federal statuses.

The Governor serves as the Commander-in-Chief of the state militia and is responsible for ordering the units into State active duty. The bill also defines the Governor's role in authorizing the militia to direct local law enforcement and the State Police.
The bill specifies that during certain exigencies and under the Governor's order, militia officers on State active duty may direct and control the Department of State Police.

The Maryland Department of Emergency Management coordinates responses to the types of disasters and public crises that trigger State active duty; clarity in the military command structure is relevant to their inter-agency coordination efforts.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Transportation Authority to design and locate the entrances, exits, and associated roads of the new bridge over the Patapsco River that will replace the collapsed Francis Scott Key Bridge to ensure that a vehicle that will not cross the bridge is not required to pay a toll.
Title: Maryland Transportation Authority - Patapsco River Toll Bridge - Design
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Transportation Authority to design and locate the entrances, exits, and associated roads of the new bridge replacing the collapsed Francis Scott Key Bridge over the Patapsco River to ensure that vehicles not crossing the bridge are not required to pay a toll.
stakeholders: Motorists and commuters using the Patapsco River bridge replacement and its surrounding road infrastructure.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Maryland Transportation Authority with the design and location of entrances and exits for the new Patapsco River bridge to ensure proper tolling procedures.
As the cabinet-level department overseeing Maryland's transportation network, the Maryland Transportation Authority operates as a key component of its multi-modal mission.
The Board must review and approve significant state expenditures and procurement contracts related to the design and construction of the new bridge.
The bridge spans the entrance to the Port of Baltimore; the road layout and entrance/exit design will significantly impact commercial truck traffic to and from maritime terminals.

The reconstruction of the Francis Scott Key Bridge is a principal executive priority, and the Governor oversees the operations of the Maryland Transportation Authority and sits on the Board of Public Works.
The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor to the Maryland Transportation Authority and will review the legal and regulatory implications of the bridge's design and tolling structure.
The Comptroller sits on the Board of Public Works to approve the significant infrastructure contracts associated with this project and serves as the state's fiscal watchdog.
The Treasurer sits on the Board of Public Works and manages the state's financial assets and debt, which may be impacted by the financing of a major bridge project.
The agency provides technical assistance on land use; the specific location of entrances, exits, and associated roads must align with state planning and sustainable growth goals.
The agency oversees environmental permitting and restoration efforts related to infrastructure construction over the Patapsco River.
The agency manages the state's fiscal accountability and will monitor the long-term budgetary impact and revenue implications for the state's transportation funds.

Synopsis: Requiring, by October 1, 2026, and each October 1 thereafter, the Office of the Attorney General to publish a handbook summarizing State law, federal law, and case law related to wearing, carrying, and transporting a handgun in public in Maryland; and requiring the handbook to be drafted in plain language so it can be easily understood without special knowledge of relevant law and in a format that can be easily used to teach certain required firearms courses.
Title: Handguns - Wear, Carry, and Transport Laws - Handbook Publication
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/17 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Office of the Attorney General to publish and annually update a handbook summarizing all state, federal, and case laws applicable to the wearing, carrying, and transporting of handguns in public. The handbook must be written in plain language and formatted for use in required firearm safety courses.
stakeholders: Maryland handgun owners, firearm safety course instructors, and individuals seeking to wear, carry, or transport handguns.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Office of the Attorney General to draft, publish, and annually update a handbook summarizing state and federal laws and case law regarding handguns.

The Maryland State Police is the primary agency responsible for enforcing handgun laws and overseeing the wear and carry permit process. The handbook is required to be formatted for use in firearm safety courses, which are regulated by the MSP as a prerequisite for permit issuance under the section of the Public Safety Article modified by this bill.

The bill creates an ongoing annual administrative and publication requirement for the Office of the Attorney General, which involves personnel time and potential fiscal costs that must be managed and approved by the Department of Budget and Management.

As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees the operations of the Office of the Attorney General and the Maryland State Police, and the Governor must sign or veto the legislation that creates this new administrative mandate.

Synopsis: Establishing that a new public record is not created if, in responding to a certain request under the Public Information Act, a custodian conducts certain data manipulation.
Title: Public Information Act - Data Manipulation
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/27 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill clarifies that a custodian of a public record does not create a new public record when they perform data compilation, extraction, querying, statistical aggregation, or other data manipulation that their database program is capable of performing to respond to a Public Information Act request.
responsible_party: Custodians of public records in Maryland State and local government units
stakeholders: Applicants for public records and State and local government custodians
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to have a material fiscal impact on State or local government operations or finances. Although some agencies requested additional staffing and software funding (ranging from approximately 97,200 to 199,700 dollars), the Department of Legislative Services determined these were unnecessary because the bill does not require custodians to perform new tasks beyond their current system capabilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Attorney General is the primary legal advisor on the Public Information Act (PIA). This bill amends the General Provisions Article of the Code, which falls directly under their advisory and manual-publishing purview.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Information Act Compliance Board (PIACB), which falls under this category, recommended the specific changes in this bill in its September 2025 annual report to clarify data manipulation rules.

DoIT establishes strategic direction and policies for state IT infrastructure. The bill centers on the capabilities of 'records database programs' for data manipulation, which involves DoIT's technical standards.

The Comptroller's Office is specifically mentioned in the fiscal note as a custodian that expects an increase in complex data queries and may require additional administrative staff to handle workload changes.

The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is highlighted in the fiscal note for its concerns regarding increased workloads for data analysts and software upgrades required to comply with the bill's data manipulation definitions.

The University System of Maryland (specifically UMCP) is noted in the fiscal note as potentially incurring significant software and staffing expenses to handle expanded data extraction and querying requests under the bill.

The Administrative Office of the Courts manages judicial records and databases. As a source of feedback in the fiscal note, they are impacted by the procedural definitions of record creation versus data manipulation.
As a major custodian of public health data, MDH provided information for the fiscal note and will be impacted operationally by how data manipulation is defined during records extraction.
MDE is identified as an information source in the fiscal note; they maintain significant regulatory databases that are frequently subject to complex PIA data requests.
DNR manages extensive environmental and licensing records. They are listed as a source in the fiscal note and will need to apply the bill's new definitions to their database operations.
This department maintains substantial data regarding housing programs and assistance; they were consulted for the fiscal note regarding the bill's impact on their data processing workload.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS). The bill impacts how they process extraction and statistical aggregation requests from their databases.
Commerce manages business-related data sets and was included as an information source in the fiscal note; the bill clarifies their duties when responding to requests for extracted data.
As a new regulatory body with significant public data interest, MCA is noted as a source in the fiscal note and is impacted by definitions of what constitutes a 'new' record during data queries.
MIA regulates the insurance industry and manages related datasets; the bill clarifies their technical obligations when applicants request searchable and analyzable electronic formats.
The PSC regulates utilities and manages technical data. They were consulted for the fiscal note and are impacted by the clarified standards for data manipulation in PIA responses.
The SBE manages the statewide voter registration database, a high-interest target for complex data extraction and queries that fall under the bill's expanded definitions of non-record-creation.

The MSP handles a large volume of PIA requests involving traffic and criminal data; the bill directly affects their operational definition of creating a record versus performing database manipulation.
The Governor's Office appoints the Public Information Act Compliance Board, whose recommendations led to this bill, and oversees the executive agencies that must implement these changes.
As the state's historical record agency, the Archives is affected by changes in the statutory definition of what constitutes a 'public record' versus a temporary data manipulation output.

Synopsis: Altering the definitions of "community association" and "local code violation" to authorize community associations to seek judicial relief for nuisance abatement in Baltimore County; requiring certain notices relating to nuisance actions to be provided to the county code enforcement agency and certain tenants and property owners; repealing a provision of law requiring a certain court to determine the amount and conditions of a bond filed by a community association in a certain nuisance action; etc.
Title: Baltimore County - Nuisance Actions - Community Association
Status: In the House - First Reading Government, Labor, and Elections

NarrowSubjects.Name: Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill modifies the criteria and procedures for community associations in Baltimore County to seek judicial relief for nuisance abatement. It eliminates specific membership size requirements for an organization to qualify as a 'community association,' updates the definition of 'local code violation' to align with the 2015 Baltimore County Code, and establishes detailed notification requirements for tenants, property owners, and the county code enforcement agency before legal action can be taken.
responsible_party: Baltimore County Department of Housing and Community Development and the Circuit Court for Baltimore County
stakeholders: Community associations, residential property owners, tenants, and residents of Baltimore County neighborhoods.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have no direct impact on state finances. Locally, it may result in a manageable increase in administrative duties for the Baltimore County Department of Housing and Community Development, which must provide written responses to nuisance notices if a property is under an active code enforcement plan. There may also be a slight increase in the volume of nuisance cases filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County, though the bill removes the court's requirement to determine bond amounts for these actions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly alters the procedural requirements and legal standards for nuisance abatement actions heard in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County. It expands standing for community associations, establishes new notice and certification requirements that must be filed with the court, and repeals the specific judicial mandate to determine bond amounts and conditions for these actions.

The bill focuses on neighborhood improvement and the abatement of nuisances related to housing and building code violations. These activities align with the department’s mission to foster neighborhood revitalization and manage community development, as nuisance properties often hinder the economic growth and sustainability of residential areas.

As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees state policy and signs legislation into law. This bill impacts public safety and community well-being initiatives by providing new legal tools for neighborhood organizations to address local blight and property code violations.

Synopsis: Providing that a manufacturer, distributor, or factory branch may not take an adverse action against a dealer for disclosing on its website that the advertised price of a vehicle is the manufacturer's minimum allowable advertised price and that the dealer may offer a lower price for the vehicle.
Title: Vehicle Laws - Manufacturers and Dealers - Prices Listed on Dealer Websites (Jack Fitzgerald Price Transparency Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.

bill_summary: The Jack Fitzgerald Price Transparency Act prohibits vehicle manufacturers, distributors, or factory branches from taking adverse action against a motor vehicle dealer for disclosing on its website that an advertised vehicle price is the manufacturer's minimum allowable advertised price and that the dealer may offer the vehicle at a lower price.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration
stakeholders: Licensed motor vehicle dealers, vehicle manufacturers, distributors, factory branches, and consumers purchasing vehicles in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The provided text does not include the Fiscal and Policy Note; therefore, specific estimates for state and local revenues and expenditures are not available.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The MVA is the primary regulator for vehicle dealers and manufacturers in Maryland. This bill directly amends the Transportation Article sections that govern the commercial relationships and advertising standards within the automotive industry, which the MVA oversees and enforces.

As the cabinet-level parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT is responsible for the overall regulatory framework of the Maryland Transportation Article, including the laws governing vehicle manufacturers and dealers.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the MVA and enforces consumer protection laws. Since the bill references false and deceptive advertising standards (Section 15-313) and regulates unfair business practices between manufacturers and dealers, the OAG would be involved in the legal enforcement and interpretation of these protections.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for various state agencies, including the MVA. If a manufacturer takes an adverse action against a dealer that leads to a regulatory dispute or licensing issue, Administrative Law Judges from the OAH would likely preside over the hearings.

Synopsis: Altering the purpose of the Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund; requiring the Comptroller to administer the Fund at the direction of the Office of Social Equity; altering requirements for a certain county plan for the distribution of funds from the Fund; requiring a county to consult with the Office to make any adjustments to the county plan; altering the requirements for a certain report on the Fund; requiring the Comptroller, in consultation with the Office, to ensure compliance with provisions of law governing the Fund; etc.
Title: Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund - Alterations
Status: In the House - First Reading Economic Matters

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.

Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.

Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill alters the administration and purpose of the Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund, requiring the Comptroller to administer the fund under the direction of the Maryland Office of Social Equity. It mandates that counties develop distribution plans in consultation with community stakeholders and the Office of Social Equity, focusing on populations and geographic areas most impacted by the disproportionate enforcement of cannabis laws. The bill specifies eligible uses for the funds, such as behavioral health, housing, and job training, while explicitly prohibiting expenditures for law enforcement agencies or activities.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of Social Equity and the Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Individuals and communities disproportionately impacted by cannabis prohibition, low-income populations, community-based organizations, and Maryland county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill modifies the governance of the Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund, which is funded through cannabis sales and use tax revenue and business conversion fees. Local jurisdictions are permitted to use up to 15% of their allocated funds for administrative expenses. The bill requires that all fund expenditures supplement existing local government appropriations and prohibits the use of money for law enforcement.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to administer the Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund, account for the fund, and pay out distributions to counties.
The Office of Social Equity, which directs the fund's administration and determines impacted communities, is an integral part of the state's cannabis regulatory framework managed by this agency.
The Governor appoints the Executive Director of the Office of Social Equity, which directs the fund's use, and the bill affects major executive branch social equity policy.
The State Treasurer is mandated to hold the fund separately and invest its money in the same manner as other state funds.
The bill requires the Office of Social Equity to consult with the Attorney General to identify the communities most impacted by disproportionate cannabis enforcement.
The bill specifically subjects the Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund to audits by this agency.
The fund provides financial support for community-based initiatives including behavioral health crisis response services.
The fund supports job training and workforce development programs within impacted communities.
The fund provides resources for educational programs, after-school programs, and truancy and absenteeism intervention.
The fund is used for housing and homelessness prevention initiatives.
The fund supports community child care and services for families impacted by incarceration.
The Office of Social Equity is required to consult with the Department of Commerce regarding the administration of the related Cannabis Business Assistance Fund.

Synopsis: Authorizing an address supplied by a commercial mail receiving agency to be designated as the principal office of a Maryland corporation, limited liability company, limited liability partnership, or limited partnership, under certain circumstances; and providing for the disclosure of certain contact information on request by a commercial mail receiving agency.
Title: Corporations and Associations - Principal Offices - Private Mailboxes
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 1:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Corporations -see also- Municipal Corps; Public Corps & Inst
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: The bill authorizes Maryland corporations, limited liability companies, limited liability partnerships, and limited partnerships to designate an address provided by a commercial mail receiving agency (CMRA) as their principal office, provided there is a valid agreement in place and the CMRA provides required contact information to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation or law enforcement upon request.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Maryland corporations, limited liability companies, limited liability partnerships, limited partnerships, and commercial mail receiving agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues increase starting in fiscal 2027 from 25 dollar filing fees collected when business entities update their principal office addresses. The State Department of Assessments and Taxation can manage implementation using existing resources. There is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes law enforcement agencies to request and receive non-public contact information from commercial mail receiving agencies, which directly aids the Maryland State Police in corporate-related investigations and service of process.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor for state agencies and law enforcement; it would be responsible for interpreting the new disclosure requirements and providing counsel on the enforcement of data requests to commercial mail receiving agencies.

As the state's tax collector, the Comptroller relies on accurate principal office addresses to establish business nexus, distribute local tax revenues, and manage tax correspondence and enforcement actions.

As the primary economic development agency, Commerce has a significant interest in policies that impact the ease of business formation and the regulatory requirements for establishing a corporate presence in Maryland.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Small and home-based businesses, a core focus of this office, frequently use commercial mailboxes for privacy and cost-efficiency; this bill provides the legal clarity necessary for these entrepreneurs to use such addresses as their principal office.

DBM is relevant due to the fiscal impact noted in the bill's fiscal note, which anticipates an increase in special fund revenues from filing fees associated with businesses changing their principal office addresses.

The Department of Labor licenses dozens of professional trades and business entities; the change in how principal offices are defined and documented directly impacts their licensing records and regulatory oversight.

The State Prosecutor investigates misconduct in government and election laws; the ability to access true contact information behind a commercial mailbox address provides a vital investigative tool for identifying responsible corporate officers.

The Secretary of State oversees the registration of charitable organizations, many of which are corporate entities that may choose to utilize commercial mail receiving agencies for their principal office under this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on public safety policy; it has a significant interest in the bill's provisions regarding corporate transparency and law enforcement access to the underlying contact information of business entities.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from being stopped, detained, or arrested for certain civil offenses while the individual is in a judicial facility or is traveling within 1 mile of a judicial facility for the purpose of attending a meeting, a hearing, or another official proceeding in the Judicial facility except under certain circumstances; establishing that evidence obtained in violation of the Act is inadmissible in a proceeding over which a State court or State or local agency has jurisdiction; etc.
Title: Judicial Facilities - Stops, Detentions, and Arrests - Limitations
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Public Buildings and Facilities -see also- Stadiums; St Hse
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: This bill prohibits law enforcement or government agents from stopping, detaining, or arresting an individual for a civil offense at a judicial facility or within one mile of one while the individual is traveling to a proceeding, unless prior notice is given to the court and the action is conducted without disrupting proceedings. These restrictions do not apply to criminal offenses, valid warrants, or contempt of court. The bill makes evidence obtained in violation of these rules inadmissible and allows affected individuals to sue for damages, while authorizing the Attorney General to seek injunctions against violators.
responsible_party: Maryland Attorney General and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Individuals attending judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings (such as litigants and witnesses), law enforcement agencies, law enforcement officers, and government agents.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's changes are not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances. While it allows for civil actions and requires the Attorney General to potentially seek injunctions, these activities are expected to be handled within existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines courthouses as primary judicial facilities and requires that law enforcement provide notice to court administrators or presiding judges before conducting certain stops or arrests. The AOC manages the administrative infrastructure and policies for these facilities.

The bill's definition of 'judicial facility' explicitly includes administrative hearing facilities. As the central agency for administrative hearings in Maryland, the OAH is a primary location impacted by the bill's restrictions on stops and detentions.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to bring civil actions to enjoin individuals or agencies from violating the Act. Additionally, the OAG is responsible for the guidance referenced in the bill's supplemental context regarding sensitive locations.

As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, its officers are 'persons' restricted by the bill from making certain stops, detentions, or arrests for civil offenses within or near judicial facilities without meeting specific notice and conduct requirements.

DGS manages state-owned facilities, including multi-agency centers used for quasi-judicial proceedings, and oversees the Maryland Capitol Police, who provide security and law enforcement at these sites and are subject to the bill's restrictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill aims to prevent the disruption of justice and the deterrence of access to courts. The OPD represents indigent clients at judicial facilities whose attendance at hearings and meetings is protected by the bill's limitations on civil arrests.
The PSC conducts quasi-judicial proceedings to regulate utilities; its hearing rooms and the surrounding areas would qualify as 'judicial facilities' under the bill's broad definition.

As an independent administrative agency that performs quasi-judicial reviews of tax disputes, its facilities and proceedings are directly subject to the bill's protections and definitions of judicial facilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency conducts quasi-judicial adjudications of state contract disputes. Its hearing locations fall under the bill's definition of judicial facilities.

The PERB conducts quasi-judicial proceedings, including investigating unfair labor practices and resolving disputes. Its facilities and the travel of individuals to its hearings are covered by the bill.
The bill includes specific exceptions for stops and detentions made for involuntary admissions and court-ordered examinations conducted by the Maryland Department of Health.

DJS is involved in juvenile justice proceedings that occur at judicial facilities. The bill contains specific exceptions for taking children into custody under the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Agents of the Division of Parole and Probation often interact with individuals at or near courthouses. These agents are 'government agents' subject to the bill's restrictions on stops and arrests for civil matters.
The Register of Wills operates within courthouses and manages probate proceedings; these offices are part of the judicial facilities where the bill's restrictions apply.

The Comptroller's facilities are defined as 'sensitive locations' in the legislation this bill supplements. Additionally, the Comptroller employs enforcement agents who are subject to the bill's restrictions.

As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees the implementation of statewide policy and the operations of law enforcement and administrative agencies affected by this legislation.

Synopsis: Authorizing an incarcerated individual to undergo a certain assessment at intake at a State correctional facility by a certain clinical professional; authorizing a certain clinical professional to make a certain recommendation about a certain incarcerated individual; and prohibiting a State correctional facility from putting a certain incarcerated individual in restrictive housing for more than 15 consecutive days in a 30-day time period unless the individual commits a certain prohibited act.
Title: Correctional Services - Restrictive Housing - Individuals With Developmental or Intellectual Disabilities
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.
Violence -see also- Domestic Violence; Hate Crimes

bill_summary: This bill allows licensed clinical professionals at State correctional facilities to assess new incarcerated individuals for developmental or intellectual disabilities during intake. If a disability is identified, the professional may recommend that the individual not be placed in restrictive housing for more than 15 consecutive days within a 30-day period. The facility must comply with this recommendation unless the individual commits a specified prohibited act, such as violence, escape, or inciting a riot.
responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals with developmental or intellectual disabilities, clinical mental health professionals, and State correctional facility staff
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services can handle the bill's requirements with existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State revenues, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for managing Maryland's adult correctional system and state prisons, DPSCS is directly tasked with implementing the bill's restrictions on restrictive housing and conducting the required intake assessments for individuals with disabilities.

This agency is the cabinet-level policy leader for the rights of Marylanders with disabilities. The bill directly impacts the treatment and protection of their constituent population within the criminal justice system.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is legally mandated to collect, analyze, and report annual data on the use of restrictive housing in Maryland. This bill creates a specific regulatory category for disabled individuals that the agency must track in its transparency reports.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent individuals within the correctional system. They advocate for the legal rights and safe conditions of confinement for their clients, specifically those with developmental and intellectual disabilities.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor to state correctional agencies and defends the state in civil rights litigation. They will provide guidance on constitutional compliance and implementation of the new restrictive housing limits.

The bill utilizes statutory definitions of disabilities managed by the Department of Health and relies on clinical professionals—whose licensing and professional standards are overseen by MDH boards—to perform intake assessments.

MCCR enforces anti-discrimination laws in public institutions. Extended restrictive housing for individuals with disabilities is a significant civil rights concern that may result in agency investigations or mediation.

OLA conducts compliance audits of the executive branch. They would likely review DPSCS records to ensure the department is following the 15-day restriction mandated by the bill for qualifying individuals.
The Governor's Office oversees all state departments involved and is responsible for signing the legislation and coordinating statewide initiatives related to public safety and disability rights.

As the state's central fiscal authority, DBM monitors the operational efficiency and budgetary resource allocation of the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services as it adapts to new housing requirements.

Synopsis: Requiring each local school system to identify, in its regular safety evaluation, issues of accessibility for individuals with disabilities; requiring local school systems to include in a certain confidential annual report instances in which a public school facility became inaccessible for a student with a disability in a manner that could impede evacuations or emergency response; and requiring a certain annual report to be confidential and limiting disclosure of the report to certain individuals.
Title: Public Schools - Individuals With Disabilities - Accessibility and Emergency Planning
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/11 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Accessibility - see also- Blind; Deaf; Disabilities; etc
Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch

bill_summary: The bill requires local school systems to identify accessibility issues for individuals with disabilities during regular school safety evaluations. It also mandates that school systems report specific instances where a public school facility became inaccessible to a student with a disability in a way that could hinder emergency evacuation or response. These annual safety reports are designated as confidential and exempt from public inspection under the Maryland Public Information Act.
responsible_party: Local school systems and the Maryland Center for School Safety
stakeholders: Public school students with disabilities, local school systems, and the Maryland Center for School Safety
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill requires local school systems to conduct additional safety evaluations and submit reporting regarding disability accessibility. It also requires the Maryland Center for School Safety to review these updated reports. While the bill text does not specify an appropriation, it imposes administrative and reporting requirements on both state and local entities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Center (MCSS) with receiving summaries of safety evaluations, receiving annual reports on school facility inaccessibility, and consulting with local school systems to update emergency plans based on identified weaknesses.

As the overarching agency for the Maryland Center for School Safety and the regulator of the public K-12 system, MSDE is primary in the implementation and oversight of these safety and accessibility requirements.

The bill explicitly requires school safety coordinators to coordinate with the IAC's facility assessment process when identifying issues that impact school safety and accessibility for individuals with disabilities.

This agency serves as the state's cross-disability policy leader. Since the bill focuses specifically on accessibility and emergency accommodations for students and individuals with disabilities, it aligns with MDOD's mandate to ensure equal access and independence.

The bill establishes specific confidentiality requirements and exemptions from the Maryland Public Information Act (PIA) for school safety reports, which would require legal guidance and defense from the OAG.

As the state’s primary authority for disaster preparedness and response coordination, MDEM has a secondary interest in school evacuation plans and emergency response protocols involving vulnerable populations.

Synopsis: Authorizing a member of the Correctional Officers' Retirement System to receive certain service credit on the redeposit of contributions from the Employees' Pension System or the Teachers' Pension System.
Title: Correctional Officers' Retirement System - Redeposit of Accumulated Contributions - Alterations
Status: In the House - First Reading Government, Labor, and Elections
bill_summary: This bill allows members of the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System (CORS) to receive service credit for previous periods of employment if they redeposit withdrawn accumulated contributions from the Employees’ Pension System or the Teachers’ Pension System, plus regular interest, in a single payment.
stakeholders: Members of the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System who previously withdrew contributions from the Employees’ Pension System or the Teachers’ Pension System.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Retirement Agency is the primary agency responsible for administering the Correctional Officers' Retirement System (CORS), the Employees' Pension System (EPS), and the Teachers' Pension System (TPS). This bill directly alters the administrative procedures for members of CORS to redeposit contributions and receive service credit within the funds they manage.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The majority of members in the Correctional Officers' Retirement System are employees of the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services. This bill impacts the retirement benefits and service credit options available to their correctional officer workforce.

As the state’s central fiscal and personnel authority, DBM oversees the statewide personnel system and the Governor’s annual budget, which includes the state's employer contributions to the retirement and pension systems affected by this legislation.

The State Treasurer serves as the custodian of the state's financial assets, including pension funds, and holds a key seat on the Board of Trustees of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System, which oversees the programs mentioned in the bill.

The Comptroller acts as a fiscal watchdog, manages the state's central payroll for the employees impacted by this bill, and sits on the Board of Trustees of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System.
The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation and overseeing the operations of the executive departments and the state budget that funds the retirement systems.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a landlord from collecting an application fee unless the rental unit is available or will become available within 30 days of receiving the application; requiring a landlord to provide certain written disclosures before accepting an application or screening fee; prohibiting a landlord from taking certain adverse actions against a prospective tenant unless a landlord provides certain written notice to the prospective tenant; prohibiting a landlord from taking certain actions relating to certain records; etc.
Title: Landlord and Tenant - Residential Housing - Rental Applications and Tenant Screening
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill establishes regulations for residential rental applications and tenant screening processes in Maryland. It prohibits landlords from charging application or screening fees for units that are not currently available or will not be available within 30 days. Landlords must provide written disclosures regarding screening criteria and reporting agencies before accepting fees. If an adverse action is taken against a prospective tenant, the landlord must provide written notice of the specific reasons and a copy of the screening report. Additionally, the bill prohibits landlords and screening services from considering or disclosing 'failure to pay rent' proceedings that did not result in a judgment or any shielded records. Violations are subject to civil penalties and enforcement under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Prospective residential tenants, residential landlords, and tenant screening service providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates civil penalties of up to $500 per violation. Because violations are designated as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, they are subject to enforcement by the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General. This may result in an increase in general fund revenues from penalties and a potential increase in expenditures for enforcement and the adoption of regulations. Tenants may also seek refunds and damages through private civil actions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly states that a violation of its provisions constitutes an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which is enforced by the Office of the Attorney General. Furthermore, the bill grants the Attorney General the authority to adopt regulations to carry out the section.

The bill restricts landlords from inquiring about or considering certain court records, such as failure to pay rent proceedings and 'shielded records' (as defined in existing Real Property statutes). The Judiciary and AOC manage these records and the Maryland Court Help Centers that assist residents with these legal processes.

As the primary state agency for residential housing policy and homelessness prevention, the Department of Housing and Community Development is a key stakeholder in legislation regulating rental applications, screening fees, and tenant-landlord relations.

The Commission on Civil Rights enforces anti-discrimination laws in housing. Regulations concerning tenant screening reports and the 'adverse actions' landlords may take based on those reports intersect with the Commission's oversight of fair housing practices and equal opportunity in public accommodations.

Synopsis: Requiring employers with 100 or more employees that reduced their workforce in the State by a least 10 employees while using automation technology to submit certain information to the Secretary of Labor concerning the number of employees employed, automation technology deployed or used, and certain employees separated from employment during the immediately preceding calendar year; requiring a certain covered employer to pay a certain assessment for each displaced employee reported by the covered employer; etc.
Title: Automation Technology Deployment Assessment and Displaced Employee Retraining Fund - Established
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Technology -see also- AeroT; BioT; EnergyT; InfoT; MedT; etc
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires employers with 100 or more employees who reduce their workforce by 10 or more people due to the deployment of automation technology (such as AI or robotics) to report these reductions to the Secretary of Labor and pay a $900 assessment per displaced employee. The revenue is deposited into the newly established Displaced Employee Retraining Fund, which provides support for training, job placement, and service programs for individuals whose jobs were replaced by technology.
stakeholders: Maryland employers with 100 or more employees, employees displaced by automation technology, and the Maryland Department of Labor.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues increase due to the collection of the $900 assessment per displaced employee and potential civil penalties ($250 per day for late reports and $250,000 for failure to pay assessments). State expenditures increase for the Maryland Department of Labor to administer the reporting and assessment system and to provide retraining and job placement services through the Displaced Employee Retraining Fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Labor is the primary official responsible for implementing the bill, including collecting the automation assessments, administering the Displaced Employee Retraining Fund, adopting regulations, and reporting outcomes to the Governor.

The bill requires the Secretary of Labor to submit an annual report to the Governor regarding the number of covered employers, displaced employees, and total assessments paid. The Governor also oversees the broader executive policy on economic opportunity and public safety.

The bill's core purpose is to fund the retraining of employees displaced by automation technology. This aligns directly with the Board's mission to create pathways to employment, remove barriers for underserved populations, and ensure workers meet the needs of evolving industries.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the Displaced Employee Retraining Fund separately and invest its money in the same manner as other state funds.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the Displaced Employee Retraining Fund, a new special, nonlapsing fund established by the legislation.

The OAG acts as the legal advisor to the Department of Labor. They would be responsible for providing legal counsel on the new regulations and potentially prosecuting or enforcing the high civil penalties ($250,000) for non-payment of assessments.

The Department of Commerce attracts and expansion of businesses in Maryland. This bill imposes a new fiscal assessment on larger employers (100+ employees) who deploy automation, which could impact business retention and the state's economic competitiveness.

DBM oversees state revenue and the formulation of the annual operating budget. The creation of a new special fund and the requirement that expenditures occur in accordance with the state budget involves their fiscal oversight.
The bill establishes significant civil penalties ($250 per day or $250,000 for non-payment). Affected employers would likely challenge these assessments through the OAH to ensure due process.

MHEC oversees postsecondary education and workforce-aligned academic growth. The Displaced Employee Retraining Fund may be used for programs that involve colleges and vocational schools regulated by the Commission.

Synopsis: Providing that a certain landlord may not refuse to rent to a prospective tenant who pays rent with the assistance of an income-based housing subsidy under certain circumstances; providing that a certain landlord may collect financial information from a perspective tenant under certain circumstances; and providing that a violation of the Act is a discriminatory housing practice and is subject to enforcement by the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights.
Title: Human Relations - Discrimination in Housing - Income-Based Housing Subsidies
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Public Benefits -see also- Housing; MedAsst;  SupplNutrAsstP

bill_summary: This bill prohibits landlords from refusing to rent to prospective tenants who use income-based housing subsidies, such as vouchers, based on their income, credit score, or certain past credit history. It classifies these actions as discriminatory housing practices and authorizes enforcement by the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights.
stakeholders: Landlords, residential rental property owners, and prospective tenants who utilize government or nonprofit income-based housing assistance.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a new discriminatory housing practice, which expands the enforcement and investigative scope of the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights. While specific expenditure figures are not provided in the text, this designation typically impacts state administrative workloads and investigative costs. There are no direct funding allocations or specific revenue impacts mentioned in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly classifies the refusal to rent to a prospective tenant using an income-based housing subsidy as a discriminatory housing practice, which the Commission is mandated to investigate and enforce.

DHCD is the primary agency responsible for administering affordable housing programs and rental subsidies; the bill directly impacts the utility and acceptance of the vouchers and certificates managed by this department.

OAH conducts formal hearings for contested cases from the Commission on Civil Rights, including housing discrimination claims, and would be responsible for adjudicating new cases arising from this act.
The OAG acts as the legal advisor to the Commission on Civil Rights and would be involved in defending the state's interpretation of these anti-discrimination laws or handling appeals.

DHS serves over one million low-income residents who rely on economic assistance and housing stability; these residents are the primary beneficiaries of the protections against subsidy-based discrimination.
Many older adults on fixed incomes utilize the housing subsidies and vouchers protected by this bill to maintain independent living and avoid displacement.

Individuals with disabilities frequently rely on federal and state housing assistance; the bill removes barriers to accessible housing by prohibiting discrimination based on subsidy status or related credit history.
Veterans often utilize specific income-based housing subsidies, such as HUD-VASH vouchers, to transition from homelessness to permanent housing, which are protected under this legislation.
The office coordinates efforts to eliminate childhood poverty and homelessness; ensuring that families can utilize housing subsidies without discrimination is a key component of their mission.
DBM is responsible for the fiscal oversight and personnel needs of the Commission on Civil Rights should the agency require additional resources to enforce these new anti-discrimination provisions.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "medical record" for purposes of law governing the confidentiality of medical records to require that certain information be recorded by a health care provider through certain means, instead of entered into the record of a patient or recipient, and to include certain electronic messages.
Title: Confidentiality of Medical Records - Definition of Medical Record
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 3:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill expands and clarifies the legal definition of 'medical record' for confidentiality purposes. It specifies that a medical record includes information recorded by a health care provider through written, electronic, or other means (including audio and video), and explicitly includes electronic messages that identify or are associated with a patient.
stakeholders: Patients, health care providers, and pharmacies
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is technical in nature and has no impact on state or local governmental finances. There is a minimal impact on small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the Health - General Article and administrator of public health programs and Medicaid, the Department of Health is the lead agency responsible for implementing and enforcing the Confidentiality of Medical Records Act, which this bill amends.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency oversees nearly 20,000 EMS clinicians who frequently transmit medical information via radio and electronic messages. The bill's expansion of the definition of 'medical record' to include electronic messages and various recording mediums directly impacts EMS record-keeping and privacy protocols.

The MHCC oversees health information technology standards and the use of electronic health records. The inclusion of electronic messages and diverse recording means in the legal definition of a medical record falls within their regulatory scope regarding IT and transparency.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office handles medical malpractice claims where the definition of what constitutes a 'medical record' is legally critical for evidence, discovery, and arbitration proceedings.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies on the interpretation and enforcement of confidentiality laws. They would be responsible for advising agencies on compliance with the expanded definition of medical records.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS provides healthcare services to incarcerated individuals. Their medical staff must ensure that electronic communications and recorded information comply with the updated confidentiality standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD frequently handles medical and mental health records in criminal, juvenile, and involuntary commitment cases. Changes to the legal definition of a medical record affect how they access and protect client information.

The MIA regulates health insurers who are subject to state and federal medical record confidentiality rules. Changes in state definitions may affect regulatory oversight of how insurers handle patient data.

The Judiciary handles medical records in various legal proceedings and maintains repositories like the Domestic Violence Central Repository. A broader definition of medical records may impact how such information is handled within the court system.
The MCA manages a registry of medical cannabis patients and caregivers, which involves handling sensitive medical information that must be kept confidential under state law.

DHS manages welfare and protective services for children and adults, which involve the collection and transmission of medical records. The updated definition affects their internal data management and privacy policies.

Through programs like the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and public guardianship, the Department of Aging handles medical information for older adults and must comply with updated confidentiality definitions.
This agency operates the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home, a skilled nursing facility that must adhere to medical record confidentiality laws for its residents.

The OAH adjudicates cases for the Department of Health and other agencies that often hinge on medical record evidence; the bill's clarification of what constitutes a record is relevant to their proceedings.

Synopsis: Requiring certain persons that receive certain State economic development assistance to make a certification each year that the person was not the subject of a certain final adverse determination  and is not currently failing to comply with certain outstanding requirements under a prior final judgment or order; requiring a certain unit of State government to initiate a pause on disbursements or approvals of certain economic development assistance or the award or renewal of certain State contracts; etc.
Title: Recipients of Economic Development Assistance or State Contracts - Certification of Compliance With State Labor Laws
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/17 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.
Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires entities receiving $100,000 or more in State economic development assistance or holding $250,000 or more in State procurement contracts to certify annually that they have not been subject to final adverse determinations regarding State labor laws and are in compliance with any prior labor-related judgments. Failure to file this certification or maintain compliance results in a temporary pause on the disbursement of funds, the approval of new assistance, and the awarding or renewal of State contracts.
responsible_party: State administering agencies, the Board of Public Works, and the Maryland Department of Commerce
stakeholders: Recipients of State economic development assistance (grants, loans, tax credits) and State procurement contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates administrative requirements for State agencies to collect and monitor annual labor law certifications. The Board of Public Works and the Department of Commerce are authorized to develop or modify electronic portals for filing. While no specific funding is appropriated, state units may incur costs for implementation and oversight. Non-compliant recipients face a temporary pause on State funding and contract renewals.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically tasks the Board of Public Works with designating the portal for electronic certifications and adopting a single-question model certification form.

As the primary economic development agency, it is specifically mentioned as a designee for the certification portal and acts as a major administering agency for the assistance programs affected by the bill.
The bill explicitly authorizes the referral of willfully false certifications to the Office of the Attorney General under the Maryland False Claims Act.
As the state's central procurement agency, DGS will be a primary 'administering agency' responsible for enforcing pauses on disbursements and renewals for contracts exceeding $250,000.
The agency manages a vast range of procurement contracts that will be subject to the new certification requirements and potential pauses on new awards or renewals.
This agency administers significant economic development assistance through grants and loans, making it an 'administering agency' required to implement the bill's compliance pauses.
The certification requirement is based on compliance with specific subtitles of the Labor and Employment Article, which are governed by this department.
As a member of the Board of Public Works and the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is involved in designating portals and overseeing the disbursement of state funds that may be paused.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Treasurer is responsible for designating the certification portal and safeguarding the fiscal integrity of the state expenditures impacted by this bill.
DBM oversees the state's procurement policy and the financial operations of the executive branch, impacting how agencies manage certification compliance and pauses.
The corporation provides economic development assistance through startup and innovation funding, which is subject to the bill's labor law certification requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency provides grants and loans that qualify as economic development assistance, requiring it to enforce the certification process and pauses mandated by the bill.
With independent procurement authority and significant contract activity, USM acts as an 'administering agency' responsible for ensuring its vendors meet the bill's certification standards.
The Authority manages major state construction and modernization contracts that will be subject to the $250,000 aggregate contract threshold for labor law certification.
The Council administers economic development grant programs (MAERDAF and RMPIF) which fall under the definition of assistance subject to the compliance certifications and pauses.
DoIT manages the state's IT infrastructure and vendor portals, which may be designated by BPW or Commerce to handle the electronic certification filings required by the bill.

SponsorPrimary: Prince George's County Delegation and Montgomery County Delegation

Sponsors.Name: Prince George's County Delegation and Montgomery County Delegation

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission and the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission to accept as a registered vendor any person that is registered through a vendor registration process as a vendor with Montgomery County or Prince George's County; and authorizing the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission and the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission to enter into certain memoranda of understanding with Montgomery County and Prince George's County.
Title: Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission and Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission – Vendor Registration PG/MC 107–26
Status: In the House - Reassigned to Government, Labor, and Elections

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Intergovernmental Cooperation -see also- AdmAgn; Cmts; etc.
Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission and the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission to accept any person registered as a vendor with Montgomery County or Prince George's County as a registered vendor. It also authorizes these commissions to enter into memoranda of understanding with the two counties to coordinate and implement the vendor registration process.
responsible_party: Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission and the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission
stakeholders: Vendors seeking to do business with bi-county agencies, the Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission, the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission, Montgomery County, and Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note was not provided in the text; however, the bill's requirements for reciprocal vendor registration and the establishment of memoranda of understanding suggest that the fiscal impact would be primarily administrative in nature for the commissions and the affected counties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly facilitates business access to government contracts by requiring two major commissions to accept county vendor registrations, which aligns with the office's mission to reduce barriers for small and minority-owned businesses.

The bill mandates administrative changes for the Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC), which is the primary land use and planning authority for the two counties and coordinates with the Department of Planning on state-level growth strategies.

The bill impacts the vendor registration process for the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC), which is one of the state's largest public water and sewer utilities under the regulatory purview of the Public Service Commission.
As the central procurement authority for the state, DGS is concerned with vendor registration standards and the integration of procurement processes across state and local agencies.

The OAG would be responsible for providing legal guidance to the commissions regarding the implementation of the new vendor registration requirements and the development of the authorized Memoranda of Understanding.
The Comptroller acts as the state's fiscal watchdog and monitors vendor compliance and registration systems to ensure the integrity of government revenue and spending.

The Board oversees major state procurement and fiscal integrity; streamlining vendor registration processes impacts the competitive bidding environment for projects involving these bi-county commissions.
By simplifying the vendor registration process, the bill supports the department's mission of creating a business-friendly environment and expanding economic opportunities for local entrepreneurs.

Synopsis: Repealing the termination date of certain provisions of law that authorize a county board of education to provide transportation to and from school for certain students using a vehicle other than a certain type of school vehicle under certain circumstances.
Title: County Boards of Education - Student Transportation - Sunset Repeal
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/11 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.
Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc

bill_summary: This bill repeals the sunset provision of a law that allows county boards of education to transport certain students using vehicles other than traditional school buses, effectively making the authorization for alternative student transportation permanent.
stakeholders: County boards of education and students requiring specialized transportation (such as those with disabilities, in foster care, or experiencing homelessness).
fiscal_impact_summary: By repealing the termination date of existing law, the bill allows local school systems to continue using more flexible and cost-effective transportation options for specific student populations. This likely results in local expenditure stability by avoiding more expensive traditional busing requirements, with no significant impact on state revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) oversees public K-12 education and the policies governing county boards of education. This bill directly impacts how these boards manage student transportation and the types of vehicles they are authorized to use.

The MVA is responsible for vehicle safety standards, driver licensing, and the regulation of vehicles used on Maryland roads. The use of non-standard vehicles for student transportation falls under their regulatory and safety oversight.

The MCSS is focused on student safety in K-12 environments. The shift in transportation standards to include non-traditional school vehicles has significant implications for student safety during transit, which is within the agency's mission.

The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation and overseeing the executive departments, such as MSDE and MDOT, that will implement the permanent extension of these transportation provisions.
The OAG provides legal counsel and reviews legislation for legal sufficiency, particularly regarding the authority of county boards and the repeal of statutory sunset provisions.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the governing body of Anne Arundel County to grant a property tax credit for real property that is located in a designated Rural Legacy Area and for which the owner has sold development rights under the Rural Legacy Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's criteria for the property tax credit are based on the Rural Legacy Program, which is primarily administered by the Department of Natural Resources.

The bill expands a tax credit framework that currently applies to agricultural land preservation programs, often coordinated with or similar to those managed by the Department of Agriculture.
This agency coordinates land use, sustainable growth, and resource conservation efforts, including the identification and management of rural legacy areas.
This multi-agency initiative focuses on sound land-use policies and protecting agricultural and forest lands through programs like the Rural Legacy Program.
This board has jurisdiction over appeals related to the rejection or dispute of property tax credits and local assessments.

The Tax Court adjudicates disputes regarding tax assessments and final decisions made by local taxing authorities concerning credits.

bill_summary: This bill extends the deadline for the Maryland Department of the Environment to submit a comprehensive report on the synthetic turf industry and disposal practices from July 1, 2026, to January 15, 2027. The study covers industry background, disposal and recycling methods, and proposals for improving waste management of synthetic turf.
stakeholders: Synthetic turf industry representatives, producers, retailers, and users (including local governments, county school systems, higher education facilities, and professional sports organizations), and local environmental and community stakeholders.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill extends the deadline for a reporting requirement established in 2024. As a deadline extension for an existing study, it does not allocate new funding and is expected to have no significant impact on state or local revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Department of the Environment to consult with 'county school systems' to conduct the study. MSDE oversees the public K-12 education system and coordinates with local school boards, making it a key stakeholder and consulting partner regarding synthetic turf fields in schools.

The Department of General Services manages the construction and maintenance of state-owned facilities. As the bill requires consultation with 'users' of synthetic turf and explores disposal and maintenance practices, DGS is relevant as the primary manager of the state infrastructure that may utilize these materials.

The bill explicitly tasks the Department of the Environment with conducting the study, consulting with stakeholders, and submitting the final report to the General Assembly. It is the primary implementing agency for this legislation.

MES provides technical services for solid waste management and recycling. The bill's requirement for a study on synthetic turf disposal methods and recycling proposals directly aligns with the operational expertise and environmental services MES provides to the state.

The Maryland Stadium Authority manages professional sports facilities and oversees major school construction projects (such as 'Built to Learn'). The bill's requirement for consultation with 'professional sports organizations' and 'school systems' regarding turf usage and disposal makes MSA a highly relevant consulting partner.

The bill requires consultation with 'higher education facilities.' As an independent public research university and a state agency that manages its own campus facilities and athletic fields, Morgan State University is a designated consulting stakeholder.
As a state-operated higher education facility with athletic infrastructure, Saint Mary's College is a named stakeholder for the required consultation regarding synthetic turf usage and management.

The University System of Maryland oversees 12 universities, which are prominent 'higher education facilities' that use and maintain synthetic turf fields. The bill mandates consultation with these facilities for the study.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is an independent commission housed within the Department of Health for administrative purposes, and its membership decisions impact the department's broader health regulatory framework.
