bill_summary: The Lower Bills and Local Power Act of 2026 requires electric transmission companies to participate in regional transmission organizations and prioritize advanced transmission technologies (ATT) in infrastructure projects. The bill establishes the Solar and Energy Storage Market Stabilization Program to provide financial assistance to clean energy projects facing funding gaps. Additionally, it directs the Maryland Department of Transportation to facilitate the siting of electricity lines and energy storage systems within highway rights-of-way and mandates $100 million in residential electricity bill refunds from the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund.
responsible_party: Public Service Commission, Maryland Energy Administration, and Maryland Department of Transportation
stakeholders: Residential electricity customers, electric companies and transmission utilities, solar and energy storage project developers, and State agencies including MDOT and MEA.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates the transfer of up to $100,000,000 from the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) to provide one-time refunds or credits to residential electricity customers in fiscal year 2027. It also authorizes the transfer of up to $10,000,000 from SEIF to fund a siting study by the Department of Transportation. The Solar and Energy Storage Market Stabilization Program will also be funded via SEIF. State revenues may increase through fair market value payments and administrative fees from utilities using highway rights-of-way.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates and funds the Solar and Energy Storage Market Stabilization Program within MEA, modifies the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) which MEA manages, and tasks the agency with technical consultation on energy infrastructure siting.

The bill significantly expands the Commission's regulatory oversight by requiring it to enforce regional transmission organization membership, evaluate advanced transmission technology implementation reports, and establish new performance-based incentives for electric utilities.

MDOT is mandated to develop leasing frameworks and safety guidelines for electricity transmission and battery storage in highway rights-of-way, lead a major siting study, and adopt governing regulations.

As an Administration bill, it reflects the Governor's core policy agenda and authorizes the Governor to execute over $110 million in budget amendments to facilitate customer refunds and energy infrastructure research.

OPC is the designated advocate for residential utility customers; the bill's focus on lowering utility bills and regulating transmission infrastructure directly impacts the proceedings OPC participates in before the Public Service Commission.

As the MDOT unit managing non-tolled state highways, SHA will be the primary agency overseeing the physical implementation and maintenance requirements for energy infrastructure sited within those rights-of-way.
DNR and its Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) are specifically named as essential consultants for the study regarding the siting of electricity lines and battery energy storage systems.

The bill requires MDOT to consult with the Department of Commerce for the energy infrastructure siting study to evaluate economic development potential and business impacts of new transmission corridors.

The bill modifies the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, which supports the Air and Radiation Administration within MDE, and aligns with MDE's mission to lead state climate change and clean energy initiatives.
DBM is responsible for managing the state's budget and will oversee the $110 million in budget amendments and fund transfers from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund specified in the legislation.

MCEC's statutory role is to provide innovative financing for clean energy technologies; the bill's focus on stabilizing solar and energy storage markets through state-funded grants and loans directly complements their mission.

The BPW must approve significant state expenditures and the use or lease of state property; the new leasing frameworks for highway rights-of-way for private energy projects will fall under their oversight.
OAG serves as the legal advisor to the PSC, MEA, and MDOT, and will be required to assist in drafting new regulations, safety guidelines, and leasing frameworks for the utility sector.
The bill's requirements for siting energy infrastructure in state-controlled property and rights-of-way extend to toll facilities managed by the MDTA.
MDP's role in coordinating land use and sustainable growth is relevant to the bill's initiative to utilize existing transportation corridors for large-scale energy infrastructure deployment.

As a multi-agency initiative coordinating sustainable growth among DNR, MDE, and Planning, this bill's focus on utilizing existing corridors for energy infrastructure aligns with its core smart growth goals.
The Comptroller acts as a fiscal watchdog for state revenue funds like the SEIF and sits on the Board of Public Works, which may review contracts related to right-of-way use.
The State Treasurer's Office is the custodian for the Strategic Energy Investment Fund and manages the state's financial assets and credit rating, which are impacted by large fund transfers.

bill_summary: The Protection From Predatory Pricing Act prohibits food retailers with at least 15,000 square feet from using dynamic pricing or consumer surveillance data to set prices for goods and services. It further prohibits the use of protected class data in a way that denies consumer advantages and prevents retailers from unilaterally changing employee benefits or rights guaranteed under collective bargaining agreements. Violations of the pricing and data sections are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General and the Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Large food retailers (at least 15,000 square feet), consumers, and employees of food retailers covered by collective bargaining agreements.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill may increase state General Fund revenues through civil and criminal penalties collected under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. The Office of the Attorney General could see increased expenditures related to enforcement and investigation. The bill also allows for private legal actions regarding labor violations, which may impact the judiciary but does not provide for a specific appropriation of state funds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates violations of the dynamic pricing and surveillance data prohibitions as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices. The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division is the lead agency responsible for enforcing the Maryland Consumer Protection Act and investigating predatory pricing practices.

The bill adds Section 4–406 to the Labor and Employment Article, prohibiting food retailers from diminishing rights or benefits guaranteed under collective bargaining agreements without mutual agreement. The Department of Labor oversees state labor relations and the economic welfare of Maryland's workforce.

This is an administration bill introduced by request, indicating it is a high-level executive priority. The Governor's Office oversees the strategic implementation of the Protection From Predatory Pricing Act and coordinates policy across departments.

The bill prohibits the use of 'protected class data' to offer or advertise goods in a way that denies advantages to consumers. The Commission on Civil Rights enforces anti-discrimination laws in public accommodations, which include large-scale food retail establishments.

The scope of the bill is defined by Section 11–206(c) of the Tax – General Article regarding tax-exempt food sales. As the state's tax collector, the Comptroller manages the revenue classifications and data used to identify which merchants qualify as 'food retailers' under this law.

The legislation imposes significant operational and technological restrictions on large-scale food retailers (minimum 15,000 square feet). The Department of Commerce tracks the regulatory impact on major business sectors and the state's retail economy.

Enforcement actions or penalties assessed by state agencies (such as the OAG or Department of Labor) against food retailers are subject to administrative review, which would be adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges at the OAH.

The Innovation Team is responsible for piloting data-driven solutions to childhood poverty and economic mobility. This administration bill targets predatory pricing, a policy area directly aligned with the team's mission to improve long-term economic outcomes for Maryland families.

Regulating food retail pricing and prohibiting dynamic pricing targets food insecurity and the economic pressures of childhood poverty, which are the primary focus areas of the Governor's Office for Children and its 'whole-of-government' approach.

DBM is responsible for assessing the fiscal impact of new legislation. The creation of new consumer protection and labor standards requires DBM to oversee the budgetary allocations for enforcement and personnel across the executive branch.

bill_summary: The Delivering Economic Competitiveness and Advancing Development Efforts (DECADE) Act renames the Economic Development Opportunities Program Account to the Strategic Closing Fund and reorganizes the administration of several state economic development programs. It transfers oversight of the RISE Zone and Build Our Future Grant programs to the Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO) and extends the sunsets for the Job Creation, Research and Development, and Employer Security Clearance Costs tax credits. Additionally, it increases maximum funding limits for several business assistance programs and redirects 1.5% of video lottery terminal proceeds to the Maryland Small Business Development Financing Fund.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Commerce, Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO), and the Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Small and minority-owned businesses, technology companies (specifically in biotechnology, quantum computing, and aerospace), higher education institutions, and film production entities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill reduces State general fund revenues by extending and expanding several tax credits through 2033. It redirects 1.5% of video lottery terminal revenues to small business financing funds, shifting resources away from the General Fund and the Education Trust Fund. It also increases the expenditure potential of various state-managed funds by raising individual project and grant caps, and modifies property tax credit structures for RISE zones.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This is an administration bill introduced at the request of the Governor. It establishes and alters major executive economic development initiatives, including the Strategic Closing Fund and various tax credits.

As the primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce is tasked with administering the new Strategic Closing Fund, the Maryland Small Business Development Financing Fund (MSBDFA), and certifying various tax credits modified by the bill.

The bill transfers the administration of the Regional Institution Strategic Enterprise (RISE) Zone Program and the Build Our Future Grant Program to MEDCO, making them a primary implementing agency for these initiatives.

The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Strategic Closing Fund and MSBDFA fund, processing electronic tax returns for investors, and administering the significant tax credit changes and refunds mandated by the bill.
The Treasurer is responsible for holding, investing, and reinvesting the money in the Strategic Closing Fund and the Maryland Small Business Development Financing Fund established by the Act.

The bill requires the Governor to provide appropriations in the budget bill for the Strategic Closing Fund and modifies the flow of state revenues into various development accounts, directly impacting the DBM's budget formulation duties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the distribution of video lottery terminal proceeds to the MSBDFA and the Small, Minority, and Women-Owned Businesses Account, which this office monitors for participation goals and procurement opportunities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the statutory distribution of proceeds from video lottery terminals (VLTs), which are regulated and overseen by this agency.

The RISE Zone Program and Build Our Future Grant Program involve 'qualified institutions' including colleges and universities. The bill coordinates these grants with higher education infrastructure for economic innovation.

The bill involves the 'Build Our Future' grant program for specialized workforce training and requires RISE zone concierges to assist businesses in accessing existing programs at the Maryland Department of Labor.

The bill targets 'eligible technology sectors' such as AI, Quantum, and Biotechnology for grants and development efforts, which aligns with the board's mission to create pipelines for high-wage, high-demand careers.
The USM universities serve as 'qualified institutions' that can anchor RISE zones and receive Build Our Future grants for innovation-related infrastructure like wet laboratories and SCIFs.
As a public research university, Morgan State qualifies as an institution for the RISE Zone program and grants for specialized technology infrastructure mentioned in the bill.
As a public institution of higher education, the college is an eligible 'qualified institution' under the modified RISE Zone and Build Our Future Grant programs.
TEDCO is specifically mentioned as an agency that the RISE zone concierge must coordinate with to assist businesses located in the innovation zones.
The bill requires coordination with MDOT through the RISE zone concierge and is relevant to infrastructure projects that may overlap with transportation connectivity in economic zones.
The bill requires coordination with DHCD through the RISE zone concierge and notes their joint management of certain community development block grants.
The bill specifically prohibits using Strategic Closing Funds for any construction, land acquisition, or sports facilities related to the Maryland Stadium Authority.

bill_summary: The Maryland Transit and Housing Opportunity Act encourages development near rail transit by automatically designating transit-oriented development (TOD) areas as enterprise zones, restricting local governments from imposing minimum parking requirements or prohibiting mixed-use development within specific distances of rail stations, and delaying the collection of local development impact fees and excise taxes until a project is completed. The bill also prioritizes state-owned land near transit for infrastructure loans and adds the use of project labor agreements as a scoring preference for projects financed by the TOD Capital Grant and Revolving Loan Fund.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation, Maryland Economic Development Corporation, and local governments
stakeholders: Real estate developers, residents living near rail transit stations, local government jurisdictions, and construction labor organizations
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local tax revenues will decrease due to the automatic designation of new enterprise zones which provide tax credits. Local governments will experience delayed cash flows from development excise taxes and impact fees, as collection is shifted from the start of construction to project completion. State expenditures for infrastructure loans and grants will be prioritized for transit-oriented projects, though no specific new funding is allocated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This is an administration bill ('By Request – Administration') that serves as a principal executive initiative to improve economic opportunity and public safety through housing and transit policy.
The bill automatically designates certain transit-oriented developments as enterprise zones, which involves tax credits and revenue collection oversight managed by the Comptroller's office.

The bill impacts state fiscal policy by altering the Strategic Infrastructure Revolving Loan Program and the Transit-Oriented Development Capital Grant and Revolving Loan Fund, requiring DBM oversight of these financial resources.

As the primary economic development agency, Commerce manages the enterprise zone program and facilitates business attraction, which is a core component of the bill's transit-oriented development strategy.

The bill specifically mandates the prioritization of redeveloping state-owned land contiguous to rail transit stations. DGS is responsible for the design, construction, maintenance, and real estate management of state-owned facilities.

The bill's primary goal is expanding housing opportunity near transit through mixed-use development and land use reform, aligning with DHCD's mission to revitalise neighborhoods and expand affordable housing.
The bill introduces 'project labor agreements' as a scoring preference for TOD projects, which falls under the regulatory and workforce development interests of the Department of Labor.
MDP coordinates state land use and sustainable growth policy. This bill significantly alters local land use authority, zoning for mixed-use development, and state-wide planning strategies.

MDOT is the primary implementing agency as the bill centers on transit-oriented development near rail stations. MDOT must approve TOD plans, and the bill directly modifies the Transportation Article regarding grant and loan funds.
The BPW must approve major state contracts and the acquisition or sale of state property, which will be necessary for the prioritized redevelopment of state-owned land near rail stations.

The bill specifically names MEDCO as the entity responsible for the Strategic Infrastructure Revolving Loan Program and tasks it with prioritizing redevelopment projects on state-owned land near transit.

This multi-agency initiative focuses on sustainable growth and sound land-use policies that direct development into existing communities, which is the fundamental objective of transit-oriented development (TOD).

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill involves the 'Sustainable Growth Subcabinet,' which is a coordinating body within the executive branch that establishes scoring standards for financial assistance for TOD projects.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Wicomico County Board of License Commissioners from issuing new Class A beer, wine, and liquor licenses to restaurants that hold Class B licenses after July 1, 2026, while allowing existing licenses to be renewed. It limits the total number of these licenses to one per county councilmanic district and requires license holders to purchase liquor exclusively from a county dispensary, removing the current option to purchase from wholesalers.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Wicomico County
stakeholders: Restaurants and Class B license holders in Wicomico County, alcoholic beverage wholesalers, Wicomico County dispensaries, and the Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill sets an annual license fee of $4,400. By shifting the license limit from three total in the county to one per councilmanic district (potentially five total), the bill may increase local license fee revenue. Additionally, requiring liquor purchases through county dispensaries rather than wholesalers will likely increase local dispensary profits while reducing revenue for private wholesalers.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly, including this bill affecting Wicomico County alcoholic beverages licenses.

The Comptroller serves as the state's tax collector and fiscal watchdog. This bill impacts alcoholic beverages licensing and retail purchase structures (mandating purchases from dispensaries rather than wholesalers), which falls under the Comptroller's oversight of revenue collection and financial reporting.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor to the General Assembly and state agencies. They are responsible for interpreting and upholding laws within the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, including the alterations to licensing rules and purchase requirements proposed in this bill.

DBM oversees the state's annual budget and personnel system. Since local boards of license commissioners are typically state-authorized entities, changes to their licensing fees and regulatory frameworks have fiscal implications that DBM monitors.

The Department of Commerce is responsible for stimulating private investment and supporting small businesses. This bill directly affects the business operations and licensing of restaurants and retailers in Wicomico County by altering Class A and Class B license regulations.

The OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits of executive branch agencies. Altering the financial relationship between license holders, wholesalers, and county dispensaries changes the fiscal procedures that OLA would audit for the local licensing board.

The Rural Maryland Council advocates for the interests of Maryland's 18 rural counties, including Wicomico County. This legislation specifically targets rural business operations and local government authority regarding alcoholic beverages.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "eligible project"; requiring an appropriation of a certain amount to the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program if the Governor appropriates less than $80,000,000 to the Community College Construction Grant Program in each fiscal year; increasing the number of grants, from 8 to 16, the Maryland Higher Education Commission may make in each fiscal year; etc.
Title: Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program - Alterations
Status: In the Senate - Hearing canceled
bill_summary: This bill modifies the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program by removing the $1,000,000 cost limit for eligible projects and increasing the number of annual grants the Maryland Higher Education Commission can award from 8 to 16. It mandates that if the Governor's appropriation for the Community College Construction Grant Program is less than $80,000,000, the difference must be appropriated to the Renewal Grant Program. Additionally, the bill removes the restriction preventing community colleges from receiving grants in consecutive fiscal years.
stakeholders: Maryland community colleges (including Baltimore City Community College), students, and faculty.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a mandated appropriation for the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program in years where the Community College Construction Grant Program receives less than $80 million. The required appropriation is the difference between $80 million and the amount provided to the construction program. This change, along with the increase in allowed grants from 8 to 16 and the removal of project cost caps, is expected to increase State expenditures for community college capital projects while providing additional funding and flexibility for local community colleges.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory and coordinating board for postsecondary education, MHEC is directly responsible for administering the grant program, reviewing master plans, and managing the increased volume of grants authorized by the bill.

This agency is identified as the entity responsible for administering the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program, overseeing project eligibility, and coordinating with community colleges on grant distribution.
The bill places a mandatory appropriation requirement on the Governor's budget, requiring specific funding levels for the program if other construction grant thresholds are not met.

DBM oversees the state's operating and capital budgets; the bill's requirement for increased and mandatory appropriations directly impacts their fiscal planning and budget formulation responsibilities.

The Board of Public Works oversees major state expenditures and procurement contracts. Facility renewal projects and capital grants for community colleges typically require Board approval to ensure fiscal accountability.

DGS manages the construction and maintenance of state-owned facilities. Since the bill includes Baltimore City Community College—a state agency—DGS may be involved in overseeing the repairs and improvements funded by these grants.

The bill requires projects to be part of a 10-year master plan. The Department of Planning provides technical assistance and reviews such plans to ensure they align with state growth and infrastructure policies.
The OAG serves as the legal advisor to MHEC and other executive agencies, providing guidance on regulatory changes and the legal aspects of grant administration and contract oversight.
As the state's fiscal watchdog and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is responsible for monitoring state spending and revenue allocations mandated by this bill.

The Treasurer's Office manages the state's banking and capital debt. The bill's impact on the capital budget requires the Treasurer's involvement in safeguarding and managing the allocation of public funds.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the insurance and liability framework for peer-to-peer (P2P) car sharing programs in Maryland. It requires these programs to ensure primary insurance coverage during car sharing periods, clarifies that the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund is not obligated to cover P2P use of vehicles that are not replacement vehicles, and allows P2P platforms to transfer monetary liability for tolls and traffic fines to the shared vehicle driver. Additionally, it removes certain protections for shared vehicle owners' personal insurance policies and excludes P2P programs from being defined as the 'owner' for traffic signal monitoring system citations.
responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration and Maryland Department of Transportation
stakeholders: Peer-to-peer car sharing platforms, shared vehicle owners, shared vehicle drivers, motor vehicle insurers, and the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly modifies the Insurance Article regarding motor vehicle liability requirements for peer-to-peer (P2P) car sharing programs, including coverage priority (primary vs. secondary), first-dollar claims payment, and the regulation of surplus lines policies used by these programs.

The bill specifically exempts the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund from the requirement to provide coverage to a shared vehicle driver for the use of a shared vehicle unless it is a 'replacement vehicle,' directly impacting the agency's liability exposure and operational mandate.

The bill amends the Transportation Article concerning security requirements for P2P car sharing, toll liability, and traffic signal monitoring systems. MDOT oversees the business units (MVA, SHA, MDTA) responsible for implementing these changes.

As a unit of MDOT, the MVA oversees vehicle registration, titling, and the enforcement of motor vehicle insurance requirements. The bill alters the legal definitions and insurance security requirements (Title 18.5) that the MVA must track for compliance.

The bill explicitly authorizes peer-to-peer car sharing programs to transfer monetary liability for tolls to the shared vehicle driver. As the agency managing the state's toll facilities and the E-ZPass system, this impacts their collection processes and enforcement against P2P shared vehicles.

The SHA manages the state's numbered highways and traffic control infrastructure. The bill's provisions regarding 'traffic control signal monitoring systems' and the definition of 'owner' for citations issued for violations recorded by such systems directly impact SHA's automated enforcement coordination.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and MDOT. Since the bill involves significant changes to liability, insurance contracts, and civil penalty enforcement for traffic violations, the OAG would be responsible for interpreting and defending these legal frameworks.

The bill modifies the definition of 'owner' for traffic signal monitoring system citations (red light cameras). These citations are processed through the court system, and changes to who can be held liable as an 'owner' affect judicial records and proceedings.

As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are involved in highway safety and the enforcement of motor vehicle laws. Changes to vehicle insurance requirements and liability for traffic violations impact their enforcement context.
The Governor is responsible for signing or vetoing this legislation, which balances the interests of the insurance industry, P2P car-sharing platforms, and public safety.

bill_summary: The bill modifies the reimbursement rates that health maintenance organizations (HMOs) must pay to nonparticipating health care providers. It replaces the previous method of using the prior calendar year's average contracted rate with a fixed historical baseline of January 31, 2019. These rates must be adjusted annually based on the change in the Medicare Economic Index (MEI) from 2019 to the current year for both evaluation and management services and other health care services.
stakeholders: Health maintenance organizations (HMOs), nonparticipating health care providers (including physicians and trauma centers), and HMO enrollees.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's adjustments to the reimbursement formula for out-of-network providers are likely to increase costs for HMOs. These increased costs may be passed on to enrollees and employers through higher insurance premiums. Consequently, there may be a fiscal impact on state and local governments that provide health insurance benefits to employees via HMO plans.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary enforcement and regulatory body for this bill. It is responsible for investigating violations, imposing penalties, and adopting implementing regulations in consultation with the Maryland Health Care Commission. It also serves as a venue for providers to file formal complaints against HMOs.

The bill mandates that the Maryland Health Care Commission conduct an annual review of health maintenance organization compliance with these reimbursement requirements and report its findings to the Maryland Insurance Administration. The commission must also be consulted during the regulatory adoption process.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines and identifies 'trauma centers' and 'trauma patients' based on designations and registries managed by the Institute. The bill explicitly requires health maintenance organizations to pay nonparticipating hospitals at the rates approved by the Health Services Cost Review Commission, which manages the state's hospital rate-setting system.

The bill amends the Health - General Article, which falls under the broad regulatory and oversight purview of the Department of Health. The changes to reimbursement rates directly affect the healthcare financing and delivery landscape managed by the department and its sub-units.

The bill grants health care providers the explicit right to enforce these reimbursement standards by filing civil actions in a court of competent jurisdiction, directly involving the judicial infrastructure and case management overseen by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

bill_summary: Senate Bill 418 enables U.S. Foreign Service members and their spouses who move to Maryland for federal work assignments to continue practicing their professions using valid licenses from other jurisdictions. To qualify, individuals must notify the state's relevant licensing board, remain in good standing with their previous licensing authorities, and adhere to Maryland's professional standards and continuing education requirements. This portability applies to most state-regulated jobs but does not include the practice of law or professions already governed by an interstate compact.
responsible_party: Maryland state licensing authorities, including agencies and professional boards within the Department of Labor, the Department of Health, and the State Department of Education.
stakeholders: U.S. Foreign Service members and their spouses who relocate to Maryland due to federal assignments or details.

The bill amends the Environment Article regarding the administration and electronic filing of tire recycling fee returns, which are processed by the Comptroller.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor to the numerous state licensing boards and agencies affected by this legislation, and would be responsible for advising them on the implementation of the new reciprocity standards.
The bill directly amends the Agriculture Article, impacting the licensing of veterinarians, pest control consultants, nutrient management planners, and milk haulers.
As the state's economic development agency, Commerce is impacted by policies that facilitate workforce entry for professionals relocating to Maryland.
The bill amends the Education Article regarding the certification of teachers and school counselors, which is overseen by MSDE.
The bill amends the Environment Article, affecting the licensing of wastewater professionals, well drillers, scrap tire haulers, and marine contractors.
The bill significantly impacts the Department of Health and its numerous health occupation boards by allowing reciprocal practice for a wide range of medical and health professionals.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the governing body of a Maryland county or the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City to create a specific subclass of personal property for qualified data centers and to establish a special property tax rate for that subclass.
responsible_party: The Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City or the governing body of a Maryland county
stakeholders: Owners and operators of qualified data centers, and local government taxing authorities in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is enabling legislation that allows local governments to set a special personal property tax rate for qualified data centers. This would result in a decrease in local property tax revenues if a county sets a rate lower than the standard personal property tax rate to provide a tax incentive. There is no direct impact on State revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees statewide economic development initiatives and infrastructure policy. This bill provides local jurisdictions with tax tools to attract data centers, which aligns with executive goals for technological growth and job creation.

The bill defines 'qualified data center' by cross-referencing Section 11-239 of the Tax - General Article, which concerns the sales and use tax exemption program managed by the Comptroller. The Comptroller's certification of a data center's qualified status would be necessary to trigger the local property tax subclass eligibility.

As the state’s central fiscal authority, DBM estimates state and local revenues. The creation of a property tax subclass for data centers and the setting of special rates could significantly impact local revenue streams and overall state economic forecasting.

The Department of Commerce is the primary agency for business attraction and economic development. Enabling counties to provide specific personal property tax relief for data centers is a strategic tool directly related to Commerce's mission to stimulate investment in the state's tech sector.

DoIT manages the strategic direction for information technology in Maryland. Data centers are the physical backbone of this infrastructure, and policies that incentivize their development impact the state's digital capacity and cybersecurity landscape.

MEDCO is responsible for facilitating large-scale industrial and infrastructure projects. Data centers are capital-intensive projects that often utilize MEDCO's financing and real estate solutions for modernization and economic growth.

The Maryland Tax Court is the highest level of administrative review for tax controversies. Disputes between data center owners and local governments regarding their classification within this new subclass or the application of the special rate would be adjudicated here.

PTAAB hears second-level appeals of property tax assessments and classifications. If a county creates this specific subclass, PTAAB would be responsible for resolving disputes regarding a property's qualification or valuation under these special provisions.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Maryland Department of Health and private health insurance entities (including nonprofit health service plans and health maintenance organizations) from imposing copayments, coinsurance, or deductibles on services provided through the Collaborative Care Model. This model integrates behavioral health services into primary care settings. An exception is provided for high-deductible health plans to ensure compliance with federal law.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Insurance Administration
stakeholders: Maryland Medical Assistance Program recipients, individuals covered by private health insurance policies or health maintenance organizations, and primary care providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill prohibits cost-sharing for the Collaborative Care Model, which is expected to increase State expenditures for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) by shifting costs from recipients to the State. For private health insurance, the prohibition on cost-sharing may result in higher premiums as insurers absorb costs previously paid by enrollees. Although the specific Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text, these mandates typically result in increased public and private healthcare expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates that the Maryland Department of Health implement and provide reimbursement for services provided under the Collaborative Care Model without imposing copayments, coinsurance, or deductibles for Medicaid (Program) recipients.

The bill adds a new section to the Insurance Article prohibiting insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs from imposing cost-sharing for the Collaborative Care Model. The MIA is the primary regulator responsible for enforcing these insurance laws and reviewing policy filings for compliance.

DBM oversees the State Employee Health and Welfare Benefits Program. The prohibition on cost-sharing for Collaborative Care Model services would likely apply to the state's health plans, potentially increasing costs for the state's healthcare budget.

The MHBE manages Maryland Health Connection, the state's insurance marketplace. The bill changes the cost-sharing requirements for health and dental plans sold through the exchange, requiring coordination and updated plan comparisons for consumers.

The OAG serves as the legal advisor to the Department of Health and the Maryland Insurance Administration. It would be responsible for providing legal counsel on the implementation of these mandates and defending the regulations if challenged.

The Governor's Office oversees all executive departments, including MDH and MIA. This bill impacts state budget priorities (formulated by the Governor) and aligns with executive initiatives related to mental health and integrated care.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a court to transfer the sentencing of a minor convicted as an adult to the juvenile court if it is determined by clear and convincing evidence that the victim of the offense had committed a sex crime or human trafficking against the minor within the preceding three months. It also prohibits life sentences without the possibility of parole for minors and allows for sentences below the mandatory minimum term.
stakeholders: Minors convicted as adults who were victims of sexual crimes or human trafficking, and the Maryland juvenile justice system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal and Policy Note was not included in the provided bill text; therefore, specific estimates for state and local revenues or expenditures are not available.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill allows minors convicted as adults to be transferred to juvenile court for sentencing and requires the juvenile court to make a juvenile disposition. The Department of Juvenile Services would be responsible for the rehabilitation, supervision, and placement of these minors following such a disposition.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Minors convicted as adults are currently under the jurisdiction of DPSCS. This bill creates a mechanism to transfer some of these individuals back to the juvenile system and prohibits life without parole for minors, directly impacting sentencing and population management within adult correctional facilities.
The judiciary is responsible for implementing the transfer process and sentencing changes. The AOC manages the administrative and fiscal infrastructure for the courts involved in these proceedings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents the majority of minors facing adult criminal charges. This bill provides new legal avenues for their clients to be sentenced in juvenile court rather than adult court, which is a significant change in defense strategy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency serves as the hub for public safety policy and advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies. This bill represents a significant shift in sentencing policy for juvenile offenders in the adult system.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor to the state and manages criminal appeals. Changes to sentencing laws for minors and the transfer of jurisdiction between courts would require legal oversight and advice.

As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees the operations of DJS and DPSCS and is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation that significantly alters state criminal justice policy.

Synopsis: Providing for the valuation of a gift card for the purpose of determining value for crimes involving theft; and prohibiting a person, with the intent to defraud another, from altering or tampering with a gift card or its packaging.
Title: Criminal Law – Theft and Fraud Crimes – Valuation and Forgery of Gift Cards
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 2/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill establishes specific criteria for the valuation of gift cards in criminal theft cases, defining the value as the greatest of the face value, the value represented by the defendant, or the actual loss incurred. It also creates a new misdemeanor, gift card forgery, which prohibits the intentional alteration or tampering with a gift card or its packaging with the intent to defraud, punishable by up to 18 months imprisonment and a fine of up to $500.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Consumers, retail merchants, gift card issuers, law enforcement agencies, and the Maryland judicial system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The creation of a new misdemeanor for gift card forgery and the standardization of gift card valuation for theft crimes is expected to result in a minimal increase in State general fund revenues from fines and a minimal increase in State and local expenditures associated with incarceration and judicial proceedings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation, including this bill which establishes new criminal penalties and valuation standards for gift card theft and forgery.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor to the State and manages criminal appeals. Additionally, its Consumer Protection Division is directly concerned with fraudulent activities like gift card tampering that harm Maryland residents.

The AOC manages the judicial infrastructure. This bill creates a new misdemeanor and specific valuation criteria that will affect how theft cases are filed, prosecuted, and recorded within the state's court system.

As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the MSP is responsible for investigating crimes such as theft and fraud. Troopers would be responsible for enforcing the new gift card forgery misdemeanor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD represents indigent individuals in criminal cases where incarceration is possible. The creation of a new misdemeanor with a sentence of up to 18 months will directly increase the agency's potential caseload.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and public safety policy. The bill's focus on defining new theft valuations and criminalizing fraud is central to their mission of reducing crime and coordinating justice policy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The DPSCS manages adult corrections and community supervision. New criminal penalties could lead to increased incarceration in local or state facilities and more individuals under the supervision of the Division of Parole and Probation.

The Department of Labor's Office of Financial Regulation protects consumers within the financial services industry. Because gift cards are prepaid financial instruments defined in the Commercial Law Article, this bill impacts the regulatory landscape of consumer financial fraud.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits employers from taking discriminatory employment actions against fire and rescue public safety employees, such as firefighters and paramedics, based on their status as a medical cannabis patient or a positive drug test, provided they have a valid certification. Employers may still prohibit on-duty cannabis use or impairment and must report any on-duty impairment to the State Emergency Medical Services Board.
responsible_party: Maryland Commission on Civil Rights and the State Emergency Medical Services Board
stakeholders: Firefighters, emergency medical technicians, cardiac rescue technicians, paramedics, and state and local fire and rescue departments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not specify a funding amount. Fiscal impact includes potential minor increases in state and local expenditures related to administrative reporting of impairment incidents to the State Emergency Medical Services Board and the handling of discrimination complaints by the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends Article 20 of the State Government Article, which is the primary anti-discrimination law enforced by the MCCR. The agency would be responsible for investigating and adjudicating complaints from fire and rescue public safety employees who allege employment discrimination based on their use of medical cannabis.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires employers to report incidents of fire and rescue public safety employees reporting to work while impaired by cannabis to the State Emergency Medical Services Board, which is housed within and overseen by MIEMSS. MIEMSS also certifies many of the professionals listed in the bill.

As the state’s central personnel authority, DBM would need to update statewide employment policies and classifications to ensure that state agencies employing fire and rescue personnel (such as the State Fire Marshal or BWI Fire & Rescue) comply with these new non-discrimination requirements.

The Maryland State Police operates the Aviation Command, which employs paramedics, and the State Fire Marshal's Office. As an employer of 'fire and rescue public safety employees' as defined in the bill, the MSP would be directly impacted by the new hiring and disciplinary restrictions.

The bill specifically identifies 'The State Airport Authority' (BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport) as an employer subject to these rules. The MAA operates the BWI Fire and Rescue Department, making them a primary implementing agency for this policy.

The bill relies on definitions, certifications, and registrations managed by the MCA. The agency’s regulatory framework for medical cannabis patients and certifying providers serves as the basis for determining which employees are protected under this act.

The PERB oversees collective bargaining and labor relations for public employees. Because this bill impacts disciplinary procedures and terms of employment for fire and rescue personnel, it may affect existing labor agreements and lead to grievances or unfair labor practice charges handled by the Board.

DNR employs personnel involved in wildland firefighting and water-based rescue. As a state employer of fire and rescue public safety staff, the agency must comply with the bill's restrictions on discriminatory actions related to medical cannabis.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies (like MSP, MAA, and DNR) that employ fire and rescue personnel and would represent the state in any civil rights or discrimination litigation resulting from this bill.

OAH would likely preside over contested cases and appeals from fire and rescue employees regarding disciplinary actions or discrimination findings initiated through state agencies or the Commission on Civil Rights.

bill_summary: Senate Bill 446 modifies the Maryland Consumer Protection Act regarding the sale and resale of tickets. It removes the requirement that taxes be included in the total ticket price shown to consumers during the purchase process, while continuing to require the disclosure of fees. The bill also establishes a private right of action for consumers, artists, or venues aggrieved by violations of ticket sale laws, authorizing courts to award economic and punitive damages up to $10,000 for a first violation and $25,000 for each subsequent violation.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General (Consumer Protection Division) and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Ticket consumers, musical groups and artists, sports teams, entertainment venues, ticket issuers, secondary ticket exchanges, and ticket resellers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's fiscal impact includes a potential minor increase in the workload of state courts due to the creation of a new private right of action for ticket sale violations. It repeals tax disclosure requirements in ticket pricing and establishes specific caps for damage awards ($10,000 or $25,000 depending on the violation history). No specific state funding or revenue allocations are provided for in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Consumer Protection Act (Title 13 of the Commercial Law Article), which is primarily enforced by the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General. The agency would be responsible for regulating the newly defined ticket disclosure requirements and enforcing the prohibition on speculative ticketing.

The Maryland Stadium Authority operates major sports and entertainment venues such as the Camden Yards Sports Complex. Under the bill, the MSA qualifies as a 'ticket issuer' and 'operator of a venue,' making it directly subject to the disclosure requirements for ticket pricing, refund mandates, and potential liability for economic and punitive damages.

The bill creates a specific private right of action for consumers, artists, and venues to sue for damages in court. The Administrative Office of the Courts is relevant as it manages the infrastructure for the judiciary, which will oversee these new civil actions and the awarding of specified economic and punitive damages.

The Department of Commerce promotes the arts, film, and tourism industries in Maryland. Since the bill regulates the sale and resale of tickets for entertainment events and provides artists with a right to sue, it directly impacts the business environment for Maryland's creative and tourism sectors.

As the independent agency that conducts formal hearings for state agencies, the OAH may be involved in adjudicating administrative enforcement cases brought by the Consumer Protection Division of the OAG regarding violations of the amended ticket sale laws.

The Comptroller is the state's tax collector. The bill specifically removes the requirement to include 'taxes' in the upfront total price of a ticket listing, which alters how tax information is presented to consumers during financial transactions.

The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation and overseeing state agencies involved in consumer protection and economic regulation. The bill modifies executive branch enforcement powers regarding trade practices.

bill_summary: This bill expands the scope of individuals and organizations to whom the Maryland Department of Human Services may disclose reports and records of child abuse and neglect. Specifically, it allows disclosure to administrators of government-operated child care centers, coaches and managers of youth sports programs, and personnel of any organization that provides supervision or care of children to assist in determining the suitability of individuals for employment or involvement with children.
stakeholders: The Maryland Department of Human Services, administrators of state and local government child care centers, youth sports program coaches and administrators, organizations providing child supervision, and individuals being screened for roles involving children.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's fiscal impact involves an increase in administrative workload for the Department of Human Services to process additional requests for child abuse and neglect records. While specific revenue or expenditure amounts are not provided in the bill text, such measures typically involve minimal fiscal impact handled within existing resources or small administrative costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary custodian of child abuse and neglect records, the Department of Human Services is the lead agency responsible for managing the expanded disclosure of these sensitive reports to the new categories of individuals and organizations authorized by the bill.

The bill authorizes disclosure of child abuse records to child care centers and school systems regulated by the Maryland State Department of Education under Title 9.5 of the Education Article to facilitate suitability and personnel decisions.

The bill explicitly allows for the disclosure of child abuse reports to practitioners in hospitals or birthing centers (which are licensed by MDH) to assist in making discharge decisions when a child is suspected to be in danger.

The bill modifies the administrative oversight of the Juvenile Justice Monitoring Unit, which is currently housed within the Office of the Attorney General, and updates its statutory authorization to access child abuse records.

The bill authorizes local and state officials responsible for juvenile services to receive child abuse reports as necessary for their official functions and affects the monitoring of facilities within the juvenile justice system.

The Chancellor of the University System of Maryland is specifically authorized by the bill to receive child abuse reports to facilitate personnel or administrative actions against employees or contractors with on-campus contact with children.

As a public institution of higher education, the University President is authorized to receive child abuse reports to carry out personnel or administrative actions following a report of abuse involving an employee or contractor.

As a public institution of higher education, the College President is authorized to receive child abuse reports to carry out personnel or administrative actions following a report of abuse involving an employee or contractor.
The Department of General Services manages state-occupied buildings; the bill authorizes the disclosure of child abuse records to administrators of child care centers located within these facilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants explicit access to child abuse and neglect reports to the State Council on Child Abuse and Neglect and the State Citizens Review Board for Children for the performance of their official duties.

The bill addresses the disclosure of child abuse reports to school officials to facilitate administrative responses following reports of suspected abuse involving students, which impacts school safety protocols overseen by the Center.

The bill references the administrative relocation of monitoring units to the Correctional Ombudsman and involves the official functions of boards and councils typically overseen by the executive department.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the County Commissioners of Carroll County to borrow up to $27,000,000 through the issuance and sale of general obligation bonds. The proceeds must be used for the construction, improvement, or development of various public facilities including roads, bridges, schools, landfills, community college facilities, water and sewer infrastructure, and parks. Additionally, the funds can be used to provide loans to volunteer fire departments for equipment and facilities and for the acquisition of agricultural land and woodland preservation easements.
stakeholders: Residents of Carroll County, volunteer fire departments in Carroll County, Carroll Community College, and agricultural landowners.
fiscal_impact_summary: Carroll County revenues increase by up to $27,000,000 from the issuance of general obligation bonds. County expenditures will increase to finance the authorized capital projects and to pay the debt service (principal and interest) on the bonds over a period of up to 30 years. The county is required to levy ad valorem taxes to cover these debt service payments. There is no direct impact on State revenues or expenditures, and the bonds are exempt from State and local taxation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the chief executive authority of Maryland, the Governor's Office is responsible for signing the legislation that authorizes Carroll County to borrow funds and issue general obligation bonds.
The Comptroller's Office is responsible for state tax administration; the bill specifically exempts the authorized bonds and interest from State and local taxation.

The Treasurer's Office monitors local government debt and manages the state's broader fiscal health, which includes tracking local bond authorizations that contribute to the state's overall taxpayer burden.

The Office of the Attorney General reviews all legislation for constitutionality and legal form, ensuring the local bond authorization complies with the Maryland Constitution and Local Government Article.
The bill authorizes the issuance of installment purchase obligations to acquire agricultural land preservation easements, a key sector regulated and supported by the Department of Agriculture.
DBM serves as the state's central fiscal authority and tracks local bond authorizations as part of its oversight of the state's long-term fiscal health and budgetary planning.

The legislation facilitates loans for volunteer fire departments' equipment and facilities, aligning with the Department's responsibility for statewide emergency preparedness and public safety coordination.
The bond proceeds fund water, sewer, and refuse disposal infrastructure, all of which fall under the environmental regulatory oversight and financial assistance programs of the MDE.
The bond specifically funds public school buildings and facilities, which are managed and funded at the state level by the IAC to ensure safe and healthy learning environments.
MHEC is the coordinating board for higher education and manages the state's relationship with community colleges, including the facilities projects for Carroll Community College funded by this bond.
The Department of Planning coordinates land use and sustainable growth strategies, including the agricultural preservation and 'smart growth' projects supported by this bond authority.
The bill authorizes funding for woodland preservation easements and parks, which are primary components of the Department's resource conservation and public land management mission.
The bond covers public works projects such as roads and bridges, intersecting with MDOT's responsibility for planning and coordinating the state's transportation network.
The bond funds public school buildings, impacting the K-12 infrastructure overseen by MSDE as part of its responsibility for the public education system.
The legislation explicitly includes the construction and improvement of library facilities, which are supported by the agency's strategic leadership and capital grant programs.
The bill authorizes funding for buildings and facilities for social and health services, which are managed or directed by the Maryland Department of Health and local health departments.

Synopsis: Extending the presumption of compensability under the workers' compensation law to include, subject to certain conditions, Carroll County correctional deputies who suffer from heart disease or hypertension resulting in partial disability or death; and altering a certain definition of "public safety employee" so as to apply a certain workers' compensation provision relating to permanent partial disability benefits to correctional deputies employed by Carroll County.
Title: Workers' Compensation - Heart Disease and Hypertension Presumption and Permanent Partial Disability - Carroll County Correctional Deputies

bill_summary: This bill allows Carroll County correctional deputies to qualify more easily for workers' compensation benefits if they develop heart disease or hypertension, establishing a presumption that these conditions are work-related. It also increases the benefit amounts for certain permanent partial disability claims by designating these deputies as public safety employees.
responsible_party: Maryland Workers' Compensation Commission and the Carroll County Sheriff's Office
stakeholders: Carroll County correctional deputies and the Carroll County Government
fiscal_impact_summary: Carroll County expenditures are expected to increase due to the presumption of compensability for heart disease and hypertension and the application of higher benefit rates for permanent partial disability claims; there is no reported impact on state revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The WCC is the primary agency responsible for adjudicating workers' compensation claims in Maryland. This bill directly alters the legal standards (the presumption of compensability and the definition of 'public safety employee') that the Commission must use to process and decide claims for Carroll County correctional deputies.

The bill explicitly discusses benefits for individuals with pre-existing heart disease or hypertension that becomes 'more severe.' The SIF is responsible for paying the portion of disability benefits that results from the combination of a pre-existing condition and a new work-related injury/occupational disease.

As Maryland's largest workers' compensation insurer and the insurer of last resort, this agency (operating as Chesapeake Employers’ Insurance Company) is responsible for managing claims and paying benefits. Statutory expansions of compensable diseases and increased benefit tiers for specific employee classes directly affect their liabilities and rate-setting.

The bill contains a specific offset provision (Section 9-503(e)) requiring that combined workers' compensation and retirement benefits do not exceed the employee's weekly salary. The SRA must coordinate benefit distributions with workers' compensation payouts to ensure compliance with this cap.

The Department of Labor oversees the economic welfare of Maryland workers and the broader Labor and Employment Article of the Maryland Code. This bill directly amends several sections of that article concerning occupational diseases and public safety employee benefits.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies involved in workers' compensation administration (WCC and SIF). They would be responsible for interpreting the new statutory language and defending the state's position in related appeals or litigation.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the departments and commissions that will implement these changes and is responsible for signing the legislation into law.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the Carroll County Office of Permits and Inspections from issuing or renewing a commercial license or permit in the county if the applicant has unpaid personal property taxes except under certain circumstances; and authorizing the Carroll County Office of Permits and Inspections to issue or renew a commercial license or permit if the applicant submits certain evidence that the applicant has paid any previously unpaid personal property taxes.
Title: Carroll County - Office of Permits and Inspections - Denial of Commercial Permit or License for Unpaid Personal Property Taxes

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Carroll County Office of Permits and Inspections from issuing or renewing commercial licenses or permits to any applicant who has unpaid personal property taxes, unless the applicant can prove the tax amount is being disputed or that the taxes have since been paid.
responsible_party: Carroll County Office of Permits and Inspections
stakeholders: Commercial license and permit applicants in Carroll County and the Carroll County local government.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase Carroll County local revenues by incentivizing the payment of delinquent personal property taxes. The administrative impact on the Carroll County Office of Permits and Inspections to verify tax status is expected to be minimal and managed within existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly, including local laws such as those governing Carroll County's permit processes.

The bill provides an exception for permit denials if the applicant has 'disputed' their unpaid personal property taxes; the Maryland Tax Court is the highest administrative body for adjudicating such tax disputes.
The OAG reviews legislation for legal sufficiency and acts as the legal advisor to the state on the implementation of local government laws enacted by the General Assembly.

The bill allows applicants to bypass a permit denial if they submit evidence that they have disputed their personal property taxes; the PTAAB is the state agency responsible for hearing these disputes.

Synopsis: Establishing that damages to be awarded for the taking of land in a condemnation proceeding include, in addition to the fair market value of the land taken, any legal, expert, or other fees or costs of the action incurred by a defendant.
Title: Eminent Domain - Just Compensation - Fees and Costs
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 2/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill expands the scope of damages awarded in eminent domain proceedings. In addition to the fair market value of the land being taken, the awarding damages must now include any legal, expert, or other fees and costs incurred by the defendant during the condemnation proceeding.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and government entities with eminent domain authority
stakeholders: Maryland property owners and State and local government agencies that utilize eminent domain.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local government expenditures are expected to increase as condemning authorities will be required to reimburse defendants for legal, expert, and other fees in addition to the fair market value of the land. There is no impact on revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Eminent domain and condemnation proceedings take place within the state court system; this bill changes the calculation of damages and awards that judges must administer.
The Board of Public Works must approve all significant state property acquisitions and expenditures; increased costs from defendant legal and expert fees would impact their fiscal oversight.
As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller oversees state revenues and expenditures that would be impacted by increased condemnation costs.

The bill explicitly references easements and land takings related to the Agriculture Article, which the Department of Agriculture manages through its resource conservation and land preservation programs.
DBM oversees the state's annual operating budget; the requirement for state agencies to pay defendant legal and expert fees in condemnation cases would increase the fiscal burden on the state budget.
DGS is the central agency for state property acquisition and real estate management; this bill would directly increase the costs of land assembly for most executive branch agencies.
DNR manages public lands and oversees environmental easements; the bill specifically references damages related to the Maryland Environmental Trust, which is housed within DNR.
The bill explicitly references the Maryland Historical Trust, a unit within the Department of Planning, regarding the valuation of and damages for land takings involving historic easements.
MDOT and its business units are the most frequent users of eminent domain in the state for highway, transit, and port infrastructure; this bill would significantly increase their project costs.
MDE manages large-scale environmental infrastructure projects, such as wastewater plants, which may require land acquisition through condemnation and would face higher costs under this bill.

The Governor's Office oversees all state departments and drafts the state budget; the significant fiscal impact on multiple state agencies makes this legislation highly relevant to executive operations.
The IAC funds and approves public school construction projects; increased land acquisition costs would impact the state funding required for school infrastructure and site planning.
MAA utilizes eminent domain for the expansion and development of state-owned airports; this bill would increase the legal and acquisition costs for these infrastructure projects.
MEDCO develops large-scale industrial and community infrastructure projects that often require land assembly; increased condemnation costs would impact their project financing and development.
MPA manages and expands maritime facilities and shipping channels; this bill would increase the fiscal burden on their land acquisition and infrastructure development efforts.
MSA has the authority to acquire land for stadiums, convention centers, and school buildings; the requirement to pay defendant fees would significantly increase their project budgets.
The Treasurer sits on the Board of Public Works and manages the state's financial assets and risk management, which are impacted by increased liabilities from legal awards in condemnation cases.
MTA frequently uses eminent domain for rail and bus transit systems; this bill would increase the costs of acquiring land and rights-of-way for public transit infrastructure.
MDTA uses eminent domain for the construction of toll facilities and bridges; this bill would increase the costs of their infrastructure projects, which are funded by toll revenues.
As a primary procurement unit and expanding research university, Morgan State may acquire land for campus development, making the increased costs of condemnation relevant to its growth.
The OAG represents state agencies in all condemnation litigation; the requirement to pay defendant fees would directly affect their litigation strategy and the legal liability of their state clients.
As an independent state agency, the college may require land acquisition for campus facilities; this bill would increase the legal and expert costs associated with such acquisitions.
SHA is a major user of eminent domain for road construction projects; this bill would directly increase project costs by requiring the payment of defendant legal and expert fees.
USM and its member universities have the authority to acquire property for campus expansion; this bill would increase the costs associated with any necessary land takings.

stakeholders: Laurel Park horse racing licensee, Arabian horse owners and breeders, the Arabian Jockey Club of America, and the Maryland State Racing Commission
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local revenues may increase minimally from taxes and fees associated with the newly authorized Arabian breed races. There is no impact on state expenditures as the bill requires purses to be funded by the licensee or sponsors rather than the thoroughbred purse account.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor encompasses the Division of Racing and the State Racing Commission, which are the primary bodies responsible for regulating horse racing operations in the state. This bill specifically requires the State Racing Commission to approve any Arabian breed races conducted at Laurel Park.

The Comptroller is the state's chief tax collector. The bill specifies that licensees conducting Arabian breed races must pay all associated taxes and fees that would otherwise be due on a thoroughbred race, impacting the revenues collected by this office.

The Department of Agriculture supports and promotes Maryland’s agricultural and equine industries. Expanding the types of breeds allowed to race at Laurel Park impacts the state's horse industry and animal health monitoring efforts.

As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Labor and the State Racing Commission. The Governor must also sign this emergency legislation for it to take immediate effect.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that all school resource officers (SROs) carry a firearm while on the premises of their assigned schools. It specifically repeals existing restrictions on Baltimore City school police officers that previously limited their authorization to carry firearms on school property to specific times or circumstances.
responsible_party: Local school systems, local law enforcement agencies, and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners
stakeholders: School resource officers, public school students and staff, local law enforcement agencies, and local school boards
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates an annual state appropriation of $10,000,000 for grants to local school systems and law enforcement agencies to support school safety requirements. Local law enforcement agencies and school systems may incur additional costs for firearm equipment and training to comply with the requirement that all SROs be armed while on school premises.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MCSS (referred to as the 'Center' in the bill) is the primary state entity responsible for developing the specialized SRO training curriculum, coordinating with local school systems, and collecting and reporting data on SRO use of force and school safety coverage.
MSDE is the parent agency for the Maryland Center for School Safety and oversees the public K-12 school systems that are required to implement these SRO mandates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the state's central hub for public safety policy and grant administration. The bill involves significant law enforcement policy regarding school safety and references the administration of safety grants for local jurisdictions.

The bill includes a mandated annual budget appropriation of $10,000,000 for grants to local school systems and law enforcement agencies to meet SRO requirements, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget.

The Governor's Office enforces state laws, signs legislation, and drafts the annual budget including the mandated SRO funding. The Governor also receives required annual reports on school safety and SRO data.

The MSP provides support to local law enforcement and is closely associated with the state's police training and standards. The bill mandates training and certification for school resource officers that must align with state law enforcement standards.

The OAG acts as the legal advisor to the Department of Education and other state agencies, providing counsel on the interpretation and implementation of law enforcement mandates such as the firearm requirement for SROs.
